A rescue system is a live environment. When you ask for it, the provider boots
it instead of your disk. It is the usual way into a dedicated server that has
no usable remote console. It is also enough to install Corium, because the image
installs itself and the rescue only has to run it.

This page gives two routes. The rescue system decides which route you get, not
you. Route A is three commands. Route B exists because some rescue systems
cannot run a container at all. The OVH rescue system is one of them.

## Before you start

- The machine is booted into its rescue system from the provider's panel, and
  you have a shell on it.
- You know which disk is the target. Both routes overwrite one whole disk.
- You have a public SSH key and the configuration that you want the node to
  have. A dedicated server has no metadata service, so both routes add these by
  hand.
- For route B, the Corium qcow2 is on the rescue system, together with
  `qemu-img`, `sgdisk`, `growpart`, `resize2fs`, `setfattr` and `getfattr`. The
  last two come from the `attr` package. Many rescue systems do not include it,
  and the OVH rescue system does not. See [downloads](/docs/install/downloads/) for the qcow2
  and for how to make sure that the file you received is correct.

## Which route

One command gives the answer:

```bash
findmnt -n /
```

If the output is `rootfs rootfs`, the rescue runs entirely from a ramfs, and
route A cannot work. No podman flag can avoid this. The kernel refuses
`pivot_root` when the current root is the initial rootfs, so every container
fails with:

```
Error: OCI runtime error: crun: pivot_root: Invalid argument
```

In that case, use route B. If the output shows a real filesystem, for example
`tmpfs`, `ext4`, or `overlay`, containers will run. Use route A. If route A
then fails, the cause is something else.

The OVH rescue is a ramfs. So the most common reason to read this page is a
route B case.

## Route A — install with podman

`bootc install to-disk` runs from inside the Corium image and writes a complete
disk: partition table, ESP, bootloader, and the ostree deployment. You do not
need to convert or resize anything afterwards.

### 1. Write the disk

> **Warning.** Make sure that you know which disk is the target before you run
> this command. `--wipe` destroys everything on the target disk, and you cannot
> recover it. A rescue system numbers disks in its own order. That order can be
> different from the order of the installed system. Also, on a machine with
> several disks, the OS is usually on the small NVMe and the data is on the
> large disks.

```bash
lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,TYPE,MODEL
```

```bash
podman run --rm --privileged --pid=host \
  -v /dev:/dev -v /var/lib/containers:/var/lib/containers \
  --security-opt label=type:unconfined_t \
  ghcr.io/corium-os/corium:0.5.0 \
  bootc install to-disk --wipe /dev/nvme0n1
```

### 2. Seed a configuration and a user

Do this step before the reboot. A dedicated server has no metadata service and
no seed device. So cloud-init finds nothing, and the node starts with no
configuration. The agent journal then shows
`no corium configuration found, leaving node unconfigured`. **cloud-init also
creates the login user**, so this node has no account for SSH. Corium ships no
root account, and its sshd drop-in sets `PermitRootLogin no`.

Since [ADR 11](/docs/decisions/adr-0011-api-on-by-default/), you can recover from this
without a second visit. The node serves its enrolment route and prints a
pairing code on the console. Then `cctl enroll --config` can tell the node what
it is. But this still needs a console, and a dedicated server rarely gives you
a usable one. So seed the configuration here anyway. Use the API only as the
fallback if you find out later that you did not.

The cheapest fix is a kernel argument. `bootc install` writes it for you, so
add it to the command in step 1, not after it:

```bash
  bootc install to-disk --wipe \
    --karg corium.config=https://boot.example.com/node-01.yaml \
    /dev/nvme0n1
```

This gives Corium its configuration, but it does not create the user. To get
both, put a NoCloud seed on the installed system instead. Before cloud-init
stops, it looks for a seed in `/var/lib/cloud/seed/nocloud`, and `ds-identify`
finds it with no extra configuration.
[Route B writes one](#2-write-the-nocloud-seed), with the SELinux labels. Mount
the root filesystem that `bootc install` created, and do the same steps there.

### 3. Reboot out of rescue

Disable rescue mode in your provider's panel and reboot. If rescue mode stays
enabled, the machine boots the rescue again, and the installed system never
runs.

## Route B — when the rescue cannot run a container

This route uses the published qcow2. It contains the same installed system that
`bootc install` produces, laid out for a 10 GiB disk. Write it, then grow the
root partition to the size of your real disk.

### 1. Write the qcow2 and grow the root

> **Warning.** Make sure that you know which disk is the target before you run
> this command. `qemu-img convert` writes directly to the raw device. It
> destroys everything on the target disk, and you cannot recover it. A rescue
> system numbers disks in its own order. That order can be different from the
> order of the installed system. Also, on a machine with several disks, the OS
> is usually on the small NVMe and the data is on the large disks.

```bash
lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,TYPE,MODEL
```

A rescue system rarely has `oras`, and it is not worth installing it to pull
one blob. The CDN copy has a plain HTTPS URL, and the release notes publish its
digest. The bytes are the same from both sources:

```bash
curl -fsSLO https://corium.b-cdn.net/corium-0.5.0-x86_64.qcow2
sha256sum corium-0.5.0-x86_64.qcow2   # must equal the digest in the release notes
```

```bash
apt-get install -y qemu-utils        # or the distribution's equivalent

qemu-img convert -O raw -p corium-0.5.0-x86_64.qcow2 /dev/nvme0n1
sync && partprobe /dev/nvme0n1

sgdisk -e /dev/nvme0n1               # move the backup GPT to the end of the real disk
growpart /dev/nvme0n1 4
e2fsck -fp /dev/nvme0n1p4
resize2fs /dev/nvme0n1p4
```

Partition 4 is the root filesystem. To make sure, run
`lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,FSTYPE,LABEL` and find the `root` label. The resize keeps
the filesystem UUID. So the bootloader entries in the image still point at the
correct place.

### 2. Write the NoCloud seed

The seed gives the node a configuration and an account for login. It must be in
place before the reboot. Mount the root filesystem and write the seed into the
`/var` of the deployment. In an ostree system, that is
`ostree/deploy/default/var`:

```bash
mount /dev/nvme0n1p4 /mnt/root
mkdir -p /mnt/root/ostree/deploy/default/var/lib/cloud/seed/nocloud
cd /mnt/root/ostree/deploy/default/var/lib/cloud/seed/nocloud

cat > meta-data <<'EOF'
instance-id: node-01
local-hostname: node-01
EOF

cat > user-data <<'EOF'
#cloud-config
users:
  - name: core
    groups: [wheel, adm, systemd-journal]
    sudo: "ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL"
    shell: /bin/bash
    ssh_authorized_keys:
      - ssh-ed25519 AAAA... you@example.com

corium:
  api:
    enabled: true
EOF
```

That `corium:` block has no role, on purpose. With a dedicated server, you
often do not know the details yet. You decide its disks, its name, and often
its role when you can see the machine. A document with no role holds the
bootstrap until you send a role:

```bash
cctl enroll <address>:7443 --code <code> --config node-01.yaml
```

If you write `role: single` here instead, the node builds a single-node cluster
when you claim it. The cluster gets a name derived from the machine ID and has
no array under it. You can want that, and `cctl` asks before it does it. But to
undo it, you must run `cctl reset` and wait as long as for a second install. See
[configuration §3.2](/docs/reference/configuration/#32-role).

The extra groups are the only difference from the `users:` block on the other
install pages. `adm` and `systemd-journal` let the account read the journals,
because there can be no other way into this machine. See
[Proxmox step 3](/docs/install/proxmox/#3-describe-the-node) for the simpler version.

> **Warning.** SELinux causes the most common failure here. Corium runs in
> enforcing mode. A rescue system that does not know SELinux creates files with
> no label, and cloud-init cannot read files with no label. A node that boots
> with an unlabeled seed behaves exactly like a node with no seed. This failure
> is the one most likely to cost you an afternoon.

Label the files by hand. The `mkdir -p` above created exactly these four paths.
So when you label them, you cover everything that the rescue system created:

```bash
cd /mnt/root/ostree/deploy/default/var/lib/cloud

for p in seed seed/nocloud seed/nocloud/meta-data seed/nocloud/user-data; do
  setfattr -n security.selinux -v "system_u:object_r:cloud_var_lib_t:s0" "$p"
done

getfattr -R -n security.selinux seed
```

The last command prints one line for each path, and each line is
`security.selinux="system_u:object_r:cloud_var_lib_t:s0"`. If a path shows
`No such attribute` instead, cloud-init cannot read it. Before the loop runs,
all four paths show this.

`/var/lib/cloud` comes from the image, and it already has its label. So the
loop does not include any directory above `seed`. Also, the loop starts from
that directory and does not use `..`, because with `..` it is easy to select
the wrong directory. Make sure that the label is correct. From that directory,
run `getfattr -n security.selinux --only-values .`. It must print the same type.
If it prints nothing, label it the same way. Label its parents too: `var_lib_t`
for `/var/lib` and `var_t` for `/var`. A directory with no label is
`unlabeled_t`, and cloud-init cannot go through it. So one parent with no label
causes the same failure as a `user-data` with no label.

> **On 0.3.3 and earlier, add one more file.** `ds-identify` decides if
> cloud-init runs at all. It runs as a systemd generator, before `/var` is
> mounted. So it cannot see the seed that you wrote, and it decides that there
> is nothing to do. The node then boots healthy but does nothing: no account,
> no API, and only a login prompt on the console. 0.3.4 and later include the
> fix. On an earlier image, write the file yourself, into the `/etc` of the
> deployment:
>
> ```bash
> E=$(ls -d /mnt/root/ostree/deploy/default/deploy/*/etc | head -1)
> echo 'policy: search,found=all,maybe=all,notfound=enabled' > "$E/cloud/ds-identify.cfg"
> setfattr -n security.selinux -v "system_u:object_r:etc_t:s0" "$E/cloud/ds-identify.cfg"
> ```
>
> The label is necessary here for the same reason as for the seed. cloud-init
> cannot read a file that it does not have permission to read.

### 3. Leave rescue mode

Unmount everything, **disable rescue mode in the provider's panel**, and
reboot. If rescue mode stays enabled, the machine boots the rescue again, and
the installed system never runs.

---

## OVH dedicated servers

The OVH rescue (`rescue12-customer`) runs from a ramfs, so route B is the route
that works. The rescue also has no overlayfs and no `pids` cgroup controller.
Those two gaps cause their own errors first, and the errors send you in the
wrong direction:

| What you see | Cause |
|---|---|
| `'overlay' is not supported over ramfs` | no overlayfs in the rescue kernel |
| `the requested cgroup controller 'pids' is not available` | The kernel was built without it. `--pids-limit=0` gets past it |
| `crun: pivot_root: Invalid argument` | The real blocker: a ramfs root |

Investigate the first two errors only until you reach the third.

The rescue also has no `attr` package. So the labels in step 2 fail with
`setfattr: command not found`. On this page, that is the one step where a
failure looks like success and costs you an afternoon. Run
`apt-get install -y attr` first. The rescue has working networking and apt.

### The UEFI boot entry

The qcow2 contains both the removable path `EFI/BOOT/BOOTX64.EFI` and
`EFI/fedora/shimx64.efi`. So a UEFI firmware finds a bootloader without help.
An explicit entry costs nothing and removes any doubt. Add it after step 1 of
route B and before you leave rescue mode:

```bash
apt-get install -y efibootmgr
efibootmgr | grep Corium             # already there? -c would add a second one
efibootmgr -c -d /dev/nvme0n1 -p 2 -L "Corium" -l '\EFI\fedora\shimx64.efi'
```

`-c` creates a new entry every time it runs. It does not update an existing
entry. So if you install a machine twice, it gets two `Corium` entries that point
at the same file. `efibootmgr -b <n> -B` deletes one. The image fixes the
partition UUIDs. So an entry that you made before a reinstall still works after
it, and usually you do not have to do it again.

Recent hardware is UEFI. To make sure for your machine, run
`[ -d /sys/firmware/efi ] && echo UEFI` from the rescue.

### Networking

OVH gives the server its address over DHCP, and the image ships no
`NetworkManager` connection profile. So the interface starts without help. You
do not have to configure anything to reach the node at the address that the
panel shows.

The BLS entry includes `console=ttyS0`. So if the node does not come back, you
can watch the boot on the OVH IPMI serial console.
